name.text: Inverse Trigonometric Functions — why the domain must be restricted

questiontext.text:
The ordinary sine function \(\sin(x)\) is not one-to-one over all real numbers, so it cannot have a genuine inverse function unless we first restrict its domain.

Which of the following best explains why this restriction is necessary?

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]
[[feedback:prt1]]

generalfeedback.text: Since \(\sin(x)\) repeats every \(2\pi\), infinitely many different \(x\)-values (e.g. \(x=\pi/6\), \(x=5\pi/6+2\pi\), etc.) all give the same \(y\)-value. An inverse function must send each input to exactly one output, so we restrict the domain of \(\sin\) (usually to \([-\pi/2,\pi/2]\)) to make it one-to-one before inverting it.
